text: In North Kolkata, on Sitaram Ghosh Street, near College Street,
each year a legendary Kali Puja unfolds—the whole city knows it as Fata Keshto's Kali Puja.
Fata Keshto—real name Krishna Chandra Dutta—
was a powerful leader of his time, yet in devotion he ran far deeper.
In 1957 he began this barowari Kali Puja under Naba Jubak Sangha—a worship that still carries his name.
Kali Puja marks Bengal's sacred Amavasya night
when lamp-light of Diwali meets worship of Mother Kali.
Here, dhak drums, conch shells, and mantras fill the night.
What sets this puja apart is strict ritual beside grand splendour.
Until Fata Keshto's Maa leaves Kumartuli, no other Kali idol may depart.
Horse-cart procession, shehnai, and a sixteen-foot deep-blue goddess arrive.
Puja runs from eight at night until dawn, with lakhs offering anjali.
Yet Maa Kali still stands in that lane—completing Kolkata's Kali Puja.
